section_summary: This section documents political realignments and internal economic conditions in Japan between April 1941 and January 1942, centering on the fall of the second Konoye cabinet in July, the composition of the third Konoye cabinet, and the eventual rise of General Hideki Tojo's military administration in October 1941. Diplomatic reports and State Department analyses evaluate the ouster of Foreign Minister Matsuoka, the attempted assassination of Baron Hiranuma, the imperial gestures supporting Konoye, and the creation of the National Defense General Headquarters under General Yamada. In addition, the file records worsening domestic conditions inside Japan, including acute food shortages and rice riots, strict transportation and commodity rationing, and restrictive police surveillance imposed on American citizens and commercial interests following Western economic freezes.

subfiles.about: Memorandum continuation recording findings on closures of the port of Kobe and dock pass restrictions imposed on Americans.
subfiles.summary: Records a follow-up conversation on April 17 between Mr. Schmidt and Mr. Houston in New York concerning inquiries originally raised by Mr. Lacques. Schmidt explained that State Department files contained no precise closure dates for the port of Kobe, though it was known to close periodically during Japanese troop movements. Furthermore, Japanese authorities had introduced a system of dock passes that was occasionally denied to American citizens and corporate employees, requiring them to obtain special permits to visit specific vessels.
subfiles.title: Department Memorandum on Closure of the Port of Kobe and Dock Pass Regulations (Continuation)
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs files

subfiles.about: State Department telegram to Tokyo reporting Ambassador Nomura's impressions of the newly installed third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Informs Ambassador Grew in Tokyo of Japanese Ambassador Nomura's remarks during a call on Acting Secretary Welles concerning the new cabinet in Tokyo. Nomura highlighted his close personal friendship with the new Foreign Minister, Admiral Toyoda, noting that Toyoda was under personal obligation to him for having convinced Nomura to accept the ambassadorial post. Nomura characterized the cabinet as stronger than its predecessor, viewing its military members as representatives of business interests and identifying Baron Hiranuma and the Navy as stabilizing factors.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 412 to Tokyo Regarding Ambassador Nomura's Views on the New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Acting Secretary Welles and Ambassador Nomura regarding the formation and character of the third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Details an evening discussion between Acting Secretary Welles and Admiral Nomura following the installation of the new Japanese cabinet. Nomura explained that he had refused Matsuoka's requests to take the Washington post for three months, only accepting upon the personal insistence of Admiral Toyoda, who now felt indebted to him. Nomura argued that the cabinet was substantially stronger and more conservative, asserting that many military ministers represented commercial interests and that Baron Hiranuma and naval representation would exert a moderating influence.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation Between Acting Secretary Welles and Japanese Ambassador Nomura Regarding the New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a circular telegram instructing American missions to discuss Japanese expansionist activities with foreign ministers.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a circular telegram sent at 10 p.m. on July 28, 1941, to American chiefs of mission in other American republics. The document contained instructions for conferring with respective ministers of foreign affairs concerning the development of Japan's expansionist policies. The original telegram is filed under decimal classification 840.51 Frozen Credits/2804a.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Circular Instructions Concerning Japanese Expansionist Activities
subfiles.to: Chiefs of Missions in the other American Republics

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting the appointment of former Ambassador Eiji Amau as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Reports an official announcement made following the cabinet meeting on August 15, 1941, regarding the appointment of Eiji Amau as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs. Amau had previously served as Japan's Ambassador to Italy. The telegram was routed for information to the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1248 on the Appointment of Eiji Amau as Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo outlining a cabinet program to tighten control over public opinion, the press, and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Tokyo press reports of a proposed cabinet plan to centralize the direction of public opinion through reorganizing the Information Board and expanding the role of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. The plan aimed to strengthen civilian confidence in national defense, mobilize national morale, guarantee minimum livelihood, and increase control over news organs. Japanese media observed that government guidance of public opinion lagged behind methods employed in Germany, Italy, Great Britain, and the United States.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1258 on Cabinet Plan for Strengthening Direction of Public Opinion

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation recording observations by National City Bank Osaka branch manager Chamberlain on conditions and public sentiment in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Records the remarks of L. W. Chamberlain, Osaka branch manager of the National City Bank of New York, during a visit to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs following a suggestion by Ambassador Grew. Chamberlain expressed optimism that war between the United States and Japan would be avoided, noting a marked improvement in Japanese public sentiment compared to six months earlier. He described acute weariness among the Japanese population over the endless China war, compounded by severe consumption restrictions, while conceding that commercial opportunities for American banks in Japan were diminishing.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with L. W. Chamberlain on Internal Conditions and Public Sentiment in Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs files

subfiles.about: Archival charge-out slip marking the withdrawal of document 894.00/1091 from Department files.
subfiles.summary: Standard Department of State charge-out slip (Form DS-1088) recording the removal of an item from decimal file 894.00/1091. It served as a temporary placeholder in the central archival file pending the document's return.
subfiles.title: Charge-Out Slip for Document 894.00/1091

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation with Japanese Embassy Secretary Takagi regarding the resignation of the second Konoye cabinet and possible successors.
subfiles.summary: Records a discussion between Frank A. Schuler, Jr. and Third Secretary Toru Takagi of the Japanese Embassy following the sudden resignation of the cabinet in Tokyo. Takagi indicated that the embassy possessed no advance information on the development and offered personal speculation that General Minami might become Prime Minister and Mamoru Shigemitsu might take the Foreign Ministry. Takagi observed that Foreign Minister Matsuoka had reached a political impasse that could only be broken by decisive action or his departure from office.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Third Secretary Takagi on Cabinet Resignation and Successor Speculation
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs files

subfiles.about: Analytical memorandum on the composition, business representation, and strategic orientation of the third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Provides a detailed analysis of the fourteen members of the third Konoye cabinet, emphasizing the repudiation of Matsuoka, the appointment of Nomura ally Admiral Toyoda, and expanded representation of big business (Sumitomo, Mitsui, North Sakhalin Oil). Langdon suggests the government's primary aim was to stabilize the domestic economy, consolidate national defense, vigorously prosecute the China war, and seek an accommodation with the United States while avoiding reckless adventurism. He also notes an alternative hypothesis that eliminating Matsuoka removed a psychological obstacle to attacking Soviet Siberia, given corporate interests dependent on Siberian resources.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on the Composition and Significance of the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: State Department instruction to Ambassador Grew enclosing a confidential memorandum of conversation between Welles and Nomura.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Instruction No. 2212 from Acting Secretary Welles to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo, providing for his strictly confidential information a clean copy of Welles's July 18 conversation with Japanese Ambassador Nomura. The enclosed memorandum records Nomura's explanations regarding the installation of the third Konoye cabinet and his personal ties to Foreign Minister Toyoda. Nomura emphasized the stabilizing role of Baron Hiranuma and the Navy and expressed hope that the reorganization would improve Japanese-American diplomatic talks.
subfiles.title: State Department Instruction No. 2212 to Ambassador Grew Enclosing Memorandum of Conversation with Ambassador Nomura

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting the resignation of Admiral Suetsugu from the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Reports a Miyako press report stating that Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu submitted his resignation as Chairman of the Central Cooperative Council of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association to Prime Minister Konoye. Suetsugu decided to withdraw from all active political posts to quietly observe the developing situation. The telegram was routed to Far Eastern Affairs, ONI, and MID.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1363 on the Resignation of Admiral Suetsugu

subfiles.about: White House transmittal memorandum requesting an appropriate State Department acknowledgment for a book presented to President Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Requests George T. Summerlin of the State Department Protocol Division to draft an appropriate acknowledgment for a book presented to President Roosevelt. Miss Tully notes that the volume itself has been retained at the White House office.
subfiles.title: White House Memorandum Requesting Acknowledgment of Book Presented to President Roosevelt

subfiles.about: Letter from Syngman Rhee presenting an advance copy of his book 'Japan Inside Out' to President Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Presents an advance copy of Syngman Rhee's volume 'Japan Inside Out' to President Roosevelt, expressing his desire to expose Japan's ultimate ambitions to the American public. Rhee offers to make corrections in a second edition if any statements conflict with facts or American foreign policy. He expresses the hope that the President will find time to examine the publication.
subfiles.title: Letter from Syngman Rhee to President Roosevelt Presenting 'Japan Inside Out'

subfiles.about: State Department letter conveying President Roosevelt's thanks to Syngman Rhee for presenting his book 'Japan Inside Out'.
subfiles.summary: A formal acknowledgment sent on behalf of President Roosevelt thanking Syngman Rhee and the Korean Commission for his letter of August 1, 1941. It conveys the President's appreciation for Rhee's courtesy in transmitting an advance copy of his book 'Japan Inside Out'.
subfiles.title: State Department Letter of Acknowledgment to Syngman Rhee

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram from Ambassador Grew concerning internal conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 1345, sent at 7 p.m. on August 29, 1941, by Ambassador Grew regarding internal conditions in Japan. The original document is filed under decimal file 740.0011 P.W./483.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Tokyo Telegram Regarding Internal Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: FBI letter transmitting confidential reports on Baron Hiranuma's political influence and succession prospects.
subfiles.summary: Transmits confidential intelligence to Assistant Secretary Berle indicating that the Portuguese Minister of Foreign Affairs was informed in May 1941 about Baron Hiranuma's influence in reactionary and government circles. The source noted that Hiranuma might be appointed Prime Minister to succeed Prince Konoye. Such an elevation was predicted to result in a diplomatic rupture with the United States and Great Britain, followed shortly by war.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter to Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Concerning Baron Hiranuma's Influence and Succession Prospects

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting three major political events in Tokyo, imperial support for the Konoye cabinet, and the establishment of General Defense Headquarters.
subfiles.summary: Transmits a detailed four-section report (accompanied by a corrected copy of Section One and an official confidential paraphrase) analyzing three significant developments in Tokyo on September 11, 1941: a suppressed liaison conference between the cabinet and military leaders, an unprecedented imperial luncheon/dinner honoring the Konoye cabinet, and the creation of a unified military command over Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Karafuto directly responsible to the Emperor under General Otozo Yamada. Grew assesses the imperial dinner as a calculated demonstration of the Emperor's support for Konoye's moderate course and negotiations with the United States, intended to counteract agitation by pro-Axis elements like Nakano and the Tohokai. The establishment of the General Defense Headquarters under Yamada is interpreted as an effort to enforce internal discipline, curb potential right-wing coups, and manage unrest resulting from American freezing orders.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1447 on Imperial Backing for Konoye and Creation of General Defense Headquarters

subfiles.about: Memorandum by Adviser on Political Relations Hornbeck analyzing the attempted assassination of Baron Hiranuma and the perils of Japanese militarism.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes the political implications of the attempted assassination of Baron Hiranuma, accompanied by a transmittal slip to Under Secretary Welles. Hornbeck argues that pervasive threats of assassination constrain Japanese high officials who oppose militarist leadership, noting that Prince Konoye is equally vulnerable and that his proposed meeting with President Roosevelt might represent a desperate bid for political survival. Hornbeck asserts that any compromise peace settlement leaving militarists in power would perpetuate political terror, concluding that international security requires the total defeat and elimination of the militaristic philosophy dominating Japan.
subfiles.title: Adviser on Political Relations Memorandum on Japanese Militarism and the Attempt on Baron Hiranuma

subfiles.about: Transcript of a Chinese shortwave radio broadcast from Chungking discussing the political significance of the attempted assassination of Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Monitors an English-language broadcast from Chungking analyzing the assassination attempt against Cabinet Minister Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma. The broadcast traces Hiranuma's evolution from a direct-action fascist and nationalist mentor into a cautious conservative who opposed a catastrophic war against the United States and Great Britain under the influence of financiers like Seihin Ikeda. It emphasizes that Hiranuma's conservative stance made him a prime target for extremist military factions and warns that the attack leaves Prince Konoye isolated and portends imminent Japanese aggression in the Pacific.
subfiles.title: Transcript of Radio Station XGOY Broadcast on the Attempted Assassination of Baron Hiranuma

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviewing the background and reputation of General Tsunetaro Ishihara.
subfiles.summary: Provides Under Secretary Welles with biographical context on General Tsunetaro Ishihara, former Vice Chief of Staff of the Kwantung Army and current commander of the Chinkai Fortress in Korea. Langdon describes Ishihara as a notorious firebrand and sinister figure feared even by his superiors, Generals Ueda and Itagaki. Ishihara was widely believed by Japanese contacts at Hsinking to have engineered the border conflicts at Changkufeng and Nomonhan.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Concerning General Tsunetaro Ishihara

subfiles.about: Telegram from Peiping reporting rumors that the East Asia League was agitating for a cabinet headed by General Ishihara.
subfiles.summary: Reports rumors circulating in Peiping that the nationalist East Asia League was agitating for the installation of a new Japanese cabinet headed by General Ishihara. The dispatch notes Ishihara's prominence within the League and his past collaboration with Doihara and Itagaki in instigating the Manchurian Incident. The telegram was repeated to Tokyo and the Department.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 1101 on East Asia League Agitation for an Ishihara Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording discussions between Secretary Hull and the Australian Minister regarding the Japanese cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a memorandum of conversation dated September 3, 1941, between Secretary of State Cordell Hull and the Australian Minister regarding Japanese-American diplomatic talks. Hull informed the Minister that affairs were coming to a showdown between the Konoye Government and military extremists, with the latter apparently gaining ground. The original memorandum is filed under decimal classification 711.94/2279.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Australian Minister's Inquiry Concerning Japanese-American Conversations

subfiles.about: War Department military intelligence bulletin evaluating recent political realignments and military command reorganization in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Transmits War Department General Staff Information Bulletin I.B. 124 (including title page, executive brief, and memorandum for the Chief of Staff) assessing political developments in Japan. General Miles interprets the Emperor's direct command of Army Headquarters, the appointment of conservative General Otozo Yamada over Defense General Headquarters, the replacement of Admiral Suetsugu by Fumio Goto, and the imperial luncheon for the cabinet as moves to bolster civilian governance and check militarist dominance. G-2 concludes that these unprecedented steps signify a marked shift away from Axis commitments and improve prospects for a peaceful resolution of Japan's international crisis.
subfiles.title: War Department Military Intelligence Information Bulletin No. 124 on Political Developments in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo detailing Foreign Office press statements on passenger inspections, drifting mines, Duff Cooper, and trade.
subfiles.summary: Reports press conference remarks by deputy spokesman Ishii concerning rigorous inspections of passengers departing Anhui, which he justified by citing severe British mistreatment of Japanese evacuees in Singapore. Ishii addressed discussions with Moscow regarding Soviet drifting mines, characterized Duff Cooper's outspoken statements as embarrassing to the British Government, and reaffirmed Japan's intention to crush the Chungking regime militarily. He also noted that trade with the Netherlands East Indies was at a standstill, though case-by-case discussions were underway.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1546 on Foreign Office Press Conference Statements

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing an article from Contemporary Japan on the third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5807 for Under Secretary Welles, highlighting an article from the August issue of Contemporary Japan. The author argued that while the formation of the third Konoye cabinet did not alter basic foreign policy, Japan's adherence to the Axis permitted substantial divergence from German and Italian objectives in the execution of its individual role under the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Summarizing Despatch No. 5807 on the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch from Tokyo analyzing an article by Toshishige Yomota in 'Contemporary Japan' on the formation and diplomacy of the third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Transmits an extensive review and critique of an article by Toshishige Yomota, editorial writer for Yomiuri Shimbun, examining the transition from the second to the third Konoye cabinet. Yomota argued that while Japan's national policy remained immutable, Matsuoka's personal methods had become obsolete, necessitating his replacement by Admiral Toyoda to handle international changes. He maintained that joint adherence to the Tripartite Pact did not obligate Japan to follow Germany blindly, while redefining international good faith as rigid consistency in pursuing national policy rather than honoring treaty commitments.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5807 Reviewing 'Contemporary Japan' Article on the Third Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum regarding the resignation dates of the Konoye cabinet and American Bureau Chief Terasaki.
subfiles.summary: Notes that according to telegraphic reports from Tokyo, Prince Konoye's entire cabinet resigned on October 16, 1941. Schmidt reports searching departmental records without finding an official dispatch giving the exact date of Hidenari Terasaki's resignation as chief of the American Bureau of the Foreign Office, though press reports announced his departure on October 28. Schmidt concludes that Terasaki likely resigned immediately following the fall of Konoye or the formation of the Tojo government.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Resignation Dates of the Konoye Cabinet and Foreign Office Bureau Chief Terasaki
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs files

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting the official announcement of the collective resignation of the third Konoye cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports an urgent official announcement released at 8:15 p.m. on October 16, 1941, stating that the entire Konoye Cabinet submitted its resignation to the Emperor at 5:00 p.m. The Emperor requested the cabinet ministers to remain in office temporarily until a successor administration could be formed.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1643 on the Resignation of the Konoye Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting that General Tojo has been designated to form a new Japanese cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Transmits an urgent announcement from Tokyo stating that Lieutenant General Hideki Tojo, Minister of War in the outgoing Konoye Cabinet, has been designated by the Emperor to form the new cabinet.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1650 on the Designation of General Tojo as Prime Minister

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram from Tokyo reporting an imperial conference and rumors identifying General Umezu as a leading candidate for Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Relays strictly confidential information from a reliable informant concerning an afternoon conference of senior political leaders before the Emperor to resolve the cabinet crisis. The informant suggested that General Yoshijiro Umezu, Commander of the Kwantung Army, was the most likely successor to Konoye because he was the only military leader possessing sufficient influence to prevent internal dissension within the Army.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1645 on Imperial Conference and Possible Succession of General Umezu

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reviewing Japanese press reactions to the cabinet resignation and Major General Okamoto's warning on negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Tokyo editorial comment on the collapse of the third Konoye cabinet from Nichi Nichi, Kokumin, Miyako, and Hochi, which stressed that national policy remained immutable and urged the formation of a unified wartime administration. The newspapers warned the Anglo-American powers against misinterpreting the crisis as a domestic ideological split or an opportunity to detach Japan from the Axis. The telegram also highlights an address by Major General Okamoto to ex-servicemen stating that while Japan sought diplomatic agreement with the United States, concessions had reached their limit and rupture was possible.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1644 on Japanese Press Comment and Major General Okamoto's Address

subfiles.about: Telegram from Berlin reporting German official and press reactions to the fall of the Konoye cabinet and the appointment of General Tojo.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the German press published brief, factual reports on the Japanese cabinet crisis, highlighting statements by Japanese spokesmen urging a vigorous foreign policy. The semi-official Dienst aus Deutschland expressed satisfaction over General Tojo's selection, noting his consistent advocacy of close collaboration among Tripartite Pact signatories and asserting there was no doubt Japan would adhere firmly to Axis principles. The commentary noted with interest that Washington and London viewed the crisis as ending Japanese-American conversations.
subfiles.title: Berlin Telegram No. 3803 on German Reaction to the Designation of General Tojo

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting the official ministerial composition of the newly formed Tojo cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the official membership list of the Tojo Cabinet announced on October 18, 1941: Lieutenant General Hideki Tojo (Prime, War, and Home Minister), Shigenori Togo (Foreign and Overseas Affairs), Okinori Kaya (Finance), Admiral Shigetaro Shimada (Navy), Michiyo Iwamura (Justice), Kunihiko Hashida (Education), Hiroya Ino (Agriculture), Shinsuke Kishi (Commerce and Industry), retired Vice Admiral Ken Terashima (Communications and Railways), Surgeon General Chikahiko Koizumi (Welfare), and Lieutenant General Teiichi Suzuki (Minister without Portfolio).
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1652 on the Composition of the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram from Berlin reporting prominent German newspaper coverage and favorable official commentary on the Tojo cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Reports that German newspapers gave prominent coverage and favorable editorial commentary to the new Tojo Cabinet, noting reported nervousness across the United States, Britain, and Australia. Dienst aus Deutschland expressed friendly interest in Tojo's initial policy statements emphasizing the conclusion of the China conflict, the Greater East Asia new order, increased Axis cooperation, and nationwide wartime preparedness. Special satisfaction was voiced in Berlin regarding the appointment of experienced diplomat Shigenori Togo as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Berlin Telegram No. 3812 on German Press Reaction to the New Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram from Chungking summarizing Chinese editorial views that the fall of Konoye portends an imminent Japanese attack on the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Transmits a survey of Chungking press opinion on the collapse of the Konoye cabinet, showing widespread consensus that the crisis resulted from Japanese militarist opposition to American talks and German successes in Russia. Chinese newspapers unanimously predicted an impending Japanese assault on Siberia, comparing Japan's opportunistic stance to that of Italy in June 1940. Editorial organs including Ta Kung Pao, Sao Tang Pao, and Hsin Hua Jih Pao urged the United States to seize the initiative by terminating talks with Tokyo, extending defense guarantees to Moscow, and dispatching heavy bombers to Siberian airfields.
subfiles.title: Chungking Telegram No. 422 on Chinese Press Predictions of a Japanese Attack on Siberia

subfiles.about: Telegram from Tokyo reporting unanimous vernacular press approval of the Tojo cabinet and an absence of bellicose rhetoric toward America.
subfiles.summary: Reports that Japanese vernacular newspapers unanimously endorsed the Tojo Cabinet, praising the ministers' administrative experience and welcoming the rapid reorganization. Commentators emphasized the retention of the War and Home Ministries by Prime Minister Tojo as a vital measure to unify defense, politics, and the citizenry into a solid national defense state. Grew notes as highly significant that editorial reaction was notably non-bellicose, avoided mentioning the United States, and completely omitted references to the Tripartite Alliance.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1653 on Japanese Press Approval of the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: FBI letter reporting intelligence on a serious rice riot in Yokkaichi and widespread food unrest throughout Japan.
subfiles.summary: Informs Assistant Secretary Berle of confidential intelligence reporting a violent rice riot in Yokkaichi, Mie Prefecture, on September 15 or 16, 1941, during which numerous individuals were injured. The FBI source indicated that similar food disturbances were occurring almost daily across Japan. This pervasive domestic distress was cited as a primary reason why the first anniversary of the Tripartite Pact was celebrated with subdued restraint.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter to Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Reporting a Rice Riot in Yokkaichi

subfiles.about: Telegram from Shanghai summarizing local foreign, Chinese, and Japanese editorial reactions to the formation of the Tojo cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Surveys editorial opinion in Shanghai across British, American, Chinese, and Japanese periodicals following the emergence of the Tojo Cabinet. Western journals like the North China Daily News and The China Press concluded that military extremists were now in complete control, rendering Pacific war virtually inevitable and extinguishing hope for diplomatic talks. In contrast, Wang Ching-wei's organ described the military cabinet as a warning to the democracies that could still preserve peace if America accommodated the New Order, while the local Japanese daily Tairiku Shimpo asserted that basic policies remained unchanged but discounted rumors of an attack on Russia.
subfiles.title: Shanghai Telegram No. 1518 Reviewing Editorial Comment on the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing a report from National City Bank on severe rationing and obstruction of foreigners in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes for Under Secretary Welles a letter from Vice President Boies C. Hart of the National City Bank transmitting an eyewitness report by an employee recently returned from Japan. The memorandum highlights increasing hardship caused by food and supply rationing among the Japanese populace. It also notes evidence of a deliberate official policy of administrative obstruction and harassment directed against foreigners seeking to depart the country.
subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on National City Bank Report Concerning Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting an eyewitness memorandum on living conditions and administrative restrictions in Japan prepared by a returned bank employee.
subfiles.summary: Transmits to Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, a copy of a confidential memorandum prepared by a National City Bank representative who recently returned to the United States from Japan. Hart suggests the detailed observations on internal conditions will be of interest and value to Department officials.
subfiles.title: Letter from Boies C. Hart to Maxwell M. Hamilton Transmitting Eyewitness Report on Japan

subfiles.about: Eyewitness memorandum detailing severe food shortages, commodity rationing, transport restrictions, and surveillance of foreigners in Kobe.
subfiles.from: Representative of the National City Bank of New York
subfiles.summary: Provides a detailed eyewitness account of deteriorating living conditions in Kobe up to late August 1941, noting that price controls failed to prevent rising living costs and led to severe food shortages. Staples including rice, fish, eggs, meat, sugar, and flour were severely rationed or unobtainable, while civilian motor transit virtually disappeared due to gasoline restrictions and conversion to charcoal burners. The report describes the heavy impact of the July 26 American freezing order on foreign residents, including the cancellation of remittance permits, mandatory use of the Japanese language on intercity telephone calls, continuous wiretapping, and stringent postal censorship.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Living Conditions, Food Rationing, and Restrictions on Foreigners in Japan (Beginning)
